title: How Much Land Does a Man Need?
author: Leo Tolstoy
translator: a new translation made for this app from the Russian original
source: Много ли человеку земли нужно (1886), public domain

body: An elder sister came from the town to visit her younger sister in the country. The elder was married to a merchant in town, the younger to a peasant in the village. The sisters drink tea and talk. The elder sister began to boast, to praise her life in town: how roomy and clean her house was, how well she dressed, how she dressed her children, what good things she ate and drank, and how she went out driving, walking and to the theatre.
The younger sister was hurt, and began to run down the merchant’s life and to praise her own peasant life.

“I wouldn’t exchange my life for yours,” she says. “We may live plainly, but we know no fear. You live more finely, but either you make a lot of money or you lose it all. As the proverb says, loss is the elder brother of gain. It happens, too, that you are rich today and tomorrow you are begging under people’s windows. Our peasant way is safer: a peasant’s life is thin, but it is long; we shall never be rich, but we shall always have enough to eat.”
The elder sister answered:
“Enough to eat, yes, with the pigs and the calves! No elegance, no manners! However hard your husband works, you will die as you live, in the dung, and your children too.”

“Well,” says the younger, “that’s our work. But we live securely; we bow to no one and fear no one. You in town live surrounded by temptations; today all is well, but tomorrow the Evil One will turn up and, look, he’ll tempt your husband to cards, or drink, or some pretty woman. And everything will go to ruin. Doesn’t that happen?”
Pakhom, the master of the house, lay on top of the stove, listening to the women chatter.

“It’s true,” he says, “the very truth. When a man like me has been turning over our mother earth since childhood, there’s no time for foolishness to get into his head. Our only trouble is that we haven’t enough land! If I had all the land I wanted, I wouldn’t be afraid of anyone, not even the Devil himself!”
The women finished their tea, chatted a little more about clothes, cleared away the cups and went to bed.

But the Devil had been sitting behind the stove and had heard everything. He was delighted that the peasant’s wife had led her husband into boasting: he boasted that if he had land, even the Devil could not take him.
“All right,” he thinks. “We’ll have a contest, you and I. I’ll give you plenty of land. And by the land I’ll take you.”
## II

Near the village lived a small landowner, a lady with three hundred acres of land. She had always lived peaceably with the peasants and did them no harm. But she hired a retired soldier as her steward, and he began to plague the peasants with fines. However careful Pakhom was, either his horse would get into her oats, or his cow would stray into her garden, or his calves would wander into her meadows: and for everything a fine.

Pakhom paid the fines, and cursed and beat his family. And Pakhom fell into a great deal of sin that summer because of this steward. He was glad when the cattle were brought into the yard for the winter: he grudged the fodder, but at least there was nothing to fear.

That winter a rumour went round that the lady was selling her land, and that the innkeeper on the high road was arranging to buy it. When the peasants heard this, they gasped. “Well,” they think, “if the innkeeper gets the land, he’ll torment us with fines worse than the lady. We can’t live without that land; we are all hemmed in by it.” The peasants went to the lady together as a commune and asked her not to sell to the innkeeper but to let them have it. They promised to pay more. The lady agreed. The peasants began to arrange to buy the whole estate as a commune; they met once and twice to discuss it, but the business did not come off. The Evil One set them at odds; they simply could not agree. And the peasants decided to buy separately, each as much as he could manage. The lady agreed to this too. Pakhom heard that a neighbour had bought fifty acres from the lady, and that she had let him pay half the money in instalments over several years. Pakhom grew envious. “They’ll buy up all the land,” he thinks, “and I’ll be left with nothing.” He began to consult his wife.
“Other people are buying,” he says. “We must buy twenty or thirty acres too. Otherwise life is impossible: the steward is crushing us with fines.”

They thought out how to buy it. They had a hundred roubles saved; they sold a foal and half their bees, hired out their son as a labourer, and borrowed some more from a brother-in-law, and they collected half the money.

Pakhom gathered the money, chose a piece of land, forty acres with a little wood on it, and went to the lady to bargain. He bargained for the forty acres, struck hands on it and paid a deposit. They went to town and signed the deed; he paid half the money and undertook to pay the rest within two years.

And so Pakhom became a man with land. Pakhom borrowed seed and sowed the land he had bought; the harvest was good. Within a year he had paid off his debts both to the lady and to his brother-in-law. And so Pakhom became a landowner: he ploughed and sowed his own land, mowed hay on his own land, cut stakes from his own land, and grazed his cattle on his own land. When Pakhom drove out to plough his own land, which was his forever, or came to look at his young crops and his meadows, he could not rejoice enough. The very grass that grew on it, and the very flowers that bloomed on it, seemed to him quite different. Before, when he used to drive across this land, it was land like any other land; but now it had become a quite special land.
## III

So Pakhom lives and rejoices. All would have been well, except that the peasants began to let their animals trample Pakhom’s corn and meadows. He asked them politely, but they would not stop: now the herdsmen would let the cows into his meadows, now the horses from the night pasture would get into his corn. Pakhom drove them out and forgave them, and did not go to law, but then he grew tired of it and began to complain to the district court. He knew it was because they were short of land, and not on purpose, that the peasants did it, but he thought: “I can’t let them get away with it, or they’ll ruin everything. They must be taught a lesson.”

He taught them a lesson once in court, and a second time; one man was fined, then another. The neighbouring peasants began to bear Pakhom a grudge, and now and then they let their animals in on purpose. Someone got into his little wood one night and cut down a dozen young lime trees for their bark. Pakhom drove through the wood and saw something white. He drove up: the stripped trunks lay thrown on the ground, and the stumps stuck up. If only the villain had cut them from the edge of the thicket and left one standing; but no, he had cleared them all in a row. Pakhom was furious. “Oh,” he thinks, “if only I knew who did it, I’d pay him back.” He thought and thought who it could be. “No one but Semka,” he thinks. He went to Semka’s yard to search, found nothing, and they only quarrelled. And Pakhom became even more certain that Semyon had done it. He lodged a complaint. They were called to court. The case was tried and tried, and the peasant was acquitted: there was no evidence. Pakhom was more offended still, and quarrelled with the village elder and the judges.
“You,” he says, “are on the side of thieves. If you lived honestly yourselves, you wouldn’t acquit thieves.”
Pakhom quarrelled with the judges and with his neighbours. They even began to threaten to set fire to his house. Pakhom now had more room on his land, but less room in the world.

And just then a rumour went round that people were moving to new lands. And Pakhom thinks: “There’s no need for me to leave my land, but if some of the others went, there would be more room for us. I would take their land for myself and add it to mine; life would be better. As it is, we’re too cramped.”

One day Pakhom was sitting at home when a peasant passing through came in. They let him stay the night and gave him something to eat, and they got talking: where was God taking him? The peasant said he was coming from the south, from beyond the Volga, where he had been working. One thing led to another, and the peasant told how people were going there to settle. He told how people from his village had settled there, joined the commune, and been given twenty-five acres of land for every man.

“And the land is such,” he says, “that when they sowed rye, the stalks were so tall you couldn’t see a horse in it, and so thick that five handfuls made a sheaf. One peasant,” he says, “came there quite poor, with nothing but his two hands, and now he has six horses and two cows.”

Pakhom’s heart caught fire. He thinks: “Why should I struggle here in this cramped place, when one can live well? I’ll sell my land and my house here; there, with the money, I’ll build and set up a whole farm. Here, in this crowding, there’s nothing but sin. Only I must go and find out all about it myself.”

When summer came he got ready and went. He went down the Volga by steamer as far as Samara, and then walked some three hundred miles on foot. He reached the place. Everything was exactly so. The peasants live spaciously, with twenty-five acres of land given to every man, and they take newcomers into the commune gladly. And if anyone has money, he can buy as much land as he likes, besides his share, to own forever, at three roubles for the very best land; buy as much as you like!

Pakhom found out everything, came home in the autumn and began to sell everything. He sold his land at a profit, sold his house, sold all his cattle, left the commune, waited for spring, and went off with his family to the new lands.
## IV

Pakhom came to the new lands with his family and joined the commune of a large village. He treated the elders to drink and put all his papers in order. They accepted Pakhom and allotted him, for five souls, a hundred and thirty-five acres of land in different fields, besides the common pasture. Pakhom built himself a house and bought cattle. He had three times as much allotted land as he had had before. And the land was good for corn. Life was ten times better than it had been in the old place. Plenty of arable land and plenty of fodder. Keep as many cattle as you like.

At first, while he was building and setting himself up, Pakhom thought it all good; but when he had settled in, even this land began to seem cramped to him. The first year Pakhom sowed wheat on his allotted land, and it came up well. He grew keen to sow wheat, but there was too little allotted land. And what there was, was not suitable. In those parts wheat is sown on virgin steppe or on fallow land. They sow it for a year or two, and then leave it until it is overgrown with feather grass again. And many people want such land, and there is not enough for all. There are quarrels over it too; the richer ones want to sow it themselves, and the poor let it to merchants to pay their taxes. Pakhom wanted to sow more. The next year he went to a merchant and rented land for a year. He sowed more, and it came up well; but it was far from the village: he had to cart the corn ten miles. He sees that in the district there are peasant merchants who live on their own farms and grow rich. “How fine it would be,” thinks Pakhom, “if I too could buy some land outright and build a farm on it. Everything would be in one place.” And Pakhom began to think how he might buy land outright.

So Pakhom lived for three years. He rented land and sowed wheat. The years were good, the wheat came up well, and money began to pile up. He could have lived on and on like this, but Pakhom grew tired of renting land from other people every year and wrangling over land: wherever there was a nice bit of land, the peasants would swoop on it at once and take it all; if you were not quick enough to buy it, you had nothing to sow. And in the third year he rented a pasture from some peasants together with a merchant, half each; they had already ploughed it, when the peasants went to law over it, and so the work was lost. “If I had land of my own,” he thinks, “I wouldn’t have to bow to anyone, and there would be no trouble.”

And Pakhom began to inquire where he could buy land outright. And he came across a peasant. The peasant had bought thirteen hundred acres, but he had gone bankrupt and was selling cheaply. Pakhom began to bargain with him. They talked and talked, and agreed on fifteen hundred roubles, half to be paid later. They had very nearly settled it when a merchant passing through stopped at Pakhom’s yard to feed his horses. They drank some tea and talked. The merchant told him he was on his way back from the far country of the Bashkirs. There, he said, he had bought from the Bashkirs some thirteen thousand acres of land. And the whole thing had cost him a thousand roubles. Pakhom began to ask questions. The merchant told him.

“All I did,” he says, “was keep the old men happy. I gave away about a hundred roubles’ worth of silk robes and carpets, and a chest of tea, and gave wine to those who drink it. And I got it for five kopecks an acre.” He shows him the deed. “The land,” he says, “runs along a river, and the whole steppe is feather grass.”
Pakhom asked him how and what.

“There is so much land there,” says the merchant, “that you couldn’t walk round it in a year: it all belongs to the Bashkirs. And the people are as simple as sheep. You can get it almost for nothing.”
“Well,” thinks Pakhom, “why should I buy thirteen hundred acres for my thousand roubles and hang a debt round my neck as well? There, for a thousand roubles, what wouldn’t I own!”

Pakhom asked how to get there, and as soon as he had seen the merchant off, he got ready to go himself. He left the house in his wife’s care, and set off with his labourer. They stopped in town and bought a chest of tea, presents and wine: everything as the merchant had said. They drove and drove, and covered more than three hundred miles. On the seventh day they came to a Bashkir camp. Everything was as the merchant had said. They all live on the steppe, by a river, in felt tents. They do not plough and they eat no bread. Their cattle and their herds of horses roam the steppe. Foals are tethered behind the tents, and twice a day the mares are driven to them; they milk the mares and make koumiss from the milk. The women churn the koumiss and make cheese, while the men do nothing but drink koumiss and tea, eat mutton and play on their pipes. They are all sleek and cheerful, and they keep holiday all summer long. They are quite unlettered people and do not know Russian, but they are friendly.

As soon as they saw Pakhom, the Bashkirs came out of their tents and gathered round their guest. An interpreter was found. Pakhom told him he had come about land. The Bashkirs were delighted; they took Pakhom and led him into a fine tent, sat him on carpets, put down-filled cushions under him, sat down round him, and began to treat him to tea and koumiss. They killed a sheep and fed him mutton. Pakhom fetched the presents from his cart and began to give them to the Bashkirs. Pakhom gave the Bashkirs presents and shared out the tea. The Bashkirs were delighted. They chattered and chattered among themselves, and then told the interpreter to speak.

“They tell me to say to you,” says the interpreter, “that they have taken a liking to you, and that it is our custom to do a guest every kindness and to give gifts in return for gifts. You have given us gifts; now tell us what of ours you like, so that we can give you a gift in return.”

“What I like best of all here,” says Pakhom, “is your land. Where we live,” he says, “the land is crowded, and the soil is worn out, but you have plenty of land, and good land. I have never seen land like it.”

The interpreter passed this on. The Bashkirs talked and talked. Pakhom does not understand what they are saying, but he sees they are cheerful; they shout something and laugh. Then they fell silent and looked at Pakhom, and the interpreter says:
“They tell me to say to you,” he says, “that in return for your kindness they will gladly give you as much land as you want. Only point to it with your hand, and it will be yours.”
They talked some more and began to argue about something. And Pakhom asked what they were arguing about. And the interpreter said:
“Some of them say they must ask their chief about the land, and that it cannot be done without him. And others say it can be done without him.”
## VI
The Bashkirs are arguing when suddenly a man comes up in a fox-fur cap. Everyone fell silent and stood up. And the interpreter says:
“This is the chief himself.”

Pakhom at once took out his best robe and presented it to the chief, with five pounds of tea as well. The chief accepted it and sat down in the place of honour. And the Bashkirs at once began to tell him something. The chief listened and listened, nodded his head for them to be quiet, and began to speak to Pakhom in Russian.
“Well,” he says, “it can be done. Take whatever you like. There is plenty of land.”
“How can I take as much as I want?” thinks Pakhom. “It has to be made secure somehow. Otherwise they’ll say it’s mine and then take it away again.”

“Thank you,” he says, “for your kind words. You have plenty of land, and I need only a little. Only I would like to know which part will be mine. It must be measured somehow and made over to me. Otherwise, life and death are in God’s hands. You good people give it to me, but your children might take it back.”
“You are right,” says the chief. “It can be made over to you.”
Pakhom began to say:
“I heard that a merchant came here. You gave him some land too, and drew up a deed; I would like the same.”
The chief understood everything.
“That can all be done,” he says. “We have a clerk, and we will go to town, and put on all the seals.”
“And what will the price be?” says Pakhom.
“We have only one price: a thousand roubles a day.”
Pakhom did not understand.
“What kind of a measure is a day? How many acres will there be in it?”
“We do not know how to reckon that,” he says. “We sell it by the day. As much as you can walk round in a day is yours, and the price of a day is a thousand roubles.”
Pakhom was astonished.
“But in a day,” he says, “one can walk round a great deal of land.”
The chief laughed.
“It will all be yours!” he says. “Only on one condition: if you do not come back the same day to the place you started from, your money is lost.”
“But how,” says Pakhom, “am I to mark where I have been?”

“We shall stand at the place you choose, and stay there, and you will go and make your circle. Take a spade with you, and mark the way wherever you need to: dig holes at the corners and pile up the turf; afterwards we shall plough a furrow from hole to hole. Make as big a circle as you like, only be back at the place you started from before the sun goes down. All that you walk round will be yours.”

Pakhom was delighted. They decided to set out early in the morning. They talked, drank more koumiss, ate more mutton, drank more tea, and night came on. They laid Pakhom to sleep on a feather bed, and the Bashkirs went away. They promised to gather at dawn the next day and ride out to the place before sunrise.
## VII

Pakhom lay on the feather bed, but could not sleep; he kept thinking about the land. “What a great stretch of land I’ll take,” he thinks. “I can walk thirty miles in a day. The days are as long as a year just now; think how much land there will be within thirty miles! The poorer land I’ll sell or let to peasants, and the best I’ll pick out and settle on myself. I’ll get two ploughs with oxen and hire two labourers; I’ll plough a hundred and fifty acres or so, and graze cattle on the rest.”

Pakhom did not sleep all night. Only just before dawn did he doze off. As soon as he dozed off, he had a dream. He dreams that he is lying in this same tent and hears someone outside cackling with laughter. And in the dream he wanted to see who it was that was laughing, and he got up and went out of the tent, and he sees that same Bashkir chief sitting in front of the tent, holding his belly with both hands, rolling about and cackling at something. He went up and asked: “What are you laughing at?” And he sees that it is not the Bashkir chief at all, but the merchant who had come to his house the other day and told him about the land. And no sooner had he asked the merchant, “Have you been here long?” than it was no longer the merchant, but the very peasant who had come from the south to his old home. And Pakhom sees that it is not the peasant either, but the Devil himself, with horns and hoofs, sitting there and cackling, and in front of him lies a man, barefoot, in a shirt and trousers. And in the dream Pakhom looked more closely: who is this man? And he sees that the man is dead, and that it is himself. Pakhom was horrified, and woke up. He woke up. “The things one dreams!” he thinks. He looked round: through the open door he saw that it was growing pale; dawn was beginning to break. “I must wake the people,” he thinks. “It’s time to go.” Pakhom got up, woke his labourer, who was sleeping in the cart, told him to harness the horses, and went to wake the Bashkirs.
“It’s time,” he says, “to go out on the steppe and measure.”
The Bashkirs got up, they all gathered, and the chief came too. The Bashkirs began to drink koumiss again and wanted to treat Pakhom to tea, but he would not wait.
“If we’re going, let’s go,” he says. “It’s time.”
## VIII

The Bashkirs got ready and set off, some on horseback, some in carts. And Pakhom and his labourer drove in their own little cart and took a spade with them. They came to the steppe just as dawn was breaking. They drove up a little hill, a *shikhan* as the Bashkirs call it. They got out of the carts, got down from their horses, and gathered in a group. The chief came up to Pakhom and pointed with his hand.
“Here,” he says, “all you can see with your eye is ours. Choose any part you like.”
Pakhom’s eyes lit up: the land was all feather grass, level as the palm of your hand, black as poppy seed, and wherever there was a hollow, there was every kind of grass, growing breast-high.
The chief took off his fox-fur cap and put it on the ground.
“This,” he says, “will be the mark. Start from here, and come back here. All that you walk round will be yours.”

Pakhom took out the money and laid it on the cap; he took off his coat and stayed in his sleeveless jacket, tightened his belt round his belly, pulled himself together, put a little bag of bread inside his jacket, tied a flask of water to his belt, pulled up the tops of his boots, took the spade from his labourer and got ready to go. He thought and thought which way to go: it was good everywhere. He thinks: “It’s all the same: I’ll go towards the sunrise.” He turned his face to the sun, stretched himself, and waited for it to appear above the edge of the earth. He thinks: “I mustn’t lose any time. It’s easier to walk while it’s cool.” As soon as the sun flashed above the edge, Pakhom swung the spade onto his shoulder and set off into the steppe.

Pakhom walked neither slowly nor fast. He went about a mile, stopped, dug a hole, and piled the pieces of turf one on another so it would be easier to see. He went on. He loosened up and began to walk faster. He went on further and dug another hole.
Pakhom looked back. The hill showed clearly in the sunlight, and the people standing on it, and the iron tyres of the cart wheels glittering.

Pakhom reckons he has walked three miles. He was getting warm; he took off his jacket, flung it over his shoulder, and went on. He went another three miles. It grew warm. He looked at the sun: it was already time for breakfast.

“One stretch is done,” thinks Pakhom. “There are four in a day; it’s too early to turn yet. But I’ll just take off my boots.” He sat down, took off his boots, stuck them in his belt and went on. Walking became easy. He thinks: “I’ll go another three miles, then I’ll start turning left. The land here is very good; it’s a pity to leave it. The further I go, the better it gets.” He went on straight ahead. He looked back: the hill was now barely visible, the people on it looked like black ants, and something was just glittering.

“Well,” thinks Pakhom, “I’ve taken enough in this direction; I must turn. Besides, I’m sweating; I’m thirsty.” He stopped, dug a bigger hole, piled up the turf, untied his flask, drank, and turned sharply to the left. He walked and walked; the grass grew tall, and it became hot.

Pakhom began to grow tired. He looked at the sun and saw that it was just noon. “Well,” he thinks, “I must rest.” Pakhom stopped and sat down. He ate some bread and drank some water, but he did not lie down: he thinks, “If I lie down, I’ll fall asleep.” He sat for a little while and went on. At first he walked easily. The food had given him strength. But it was very hot by now, and he was getting sleepy; still he walks on, thinking: “An hour to suffer, a lifetime to live.”

He went a long way in this direction too, and was about to turn left again, when he sees a damp hollow; it’s a pity to leave it out. He thinks: “Flax would grow well here.” Again he went straight on. He took in the hollow, dug a hole beyond it, and turned the second corner. Pakhom looked back at the hill: it was hazy from the heat, something was quivering in the air, and through the shimmer the people on the hill could barely be seen: they must be ten miles away. “Well,” thinks Pakhom, “I’ve made the sides too long; I must make this one shorter.” He started along the third side and began to walk faster. He looked at the sun: it was already getting on for the afternoon, and he had gone only a mile and a half along the third side. And it was still the same ten miles back to the starting place. “No,” he thinks, “even if my land is lopsided, I must go straight back now to be in time. I mustn’t take too much. I have plenty of land as it is.” Pakhom quickly dug a hole and turned straight towards the hill.
## IX

Pakhom goes straight towards the hill, and it has become hard for him. He is soaked with sweat, his bare feet are cut and bruised, and his legs have begun to give way. He longs to rest, but he cannot: he won’t get back before sunset. The sun does not wait; it keeps sinking and sinking. “Oh,” he thinks, “have I made a mistake? Have I taken too much? What if I am not in time?” He looks ahead at the hill, he looks at the sun: the starting place is far away, and the sun is not far from the edge.

So Pakhom goes on; it is hard for him, but he keeps walking faster and faster. He walked and walked, and it was still far; he broke into a run. He threw away his jacket, his boots, his flask; he threw away his cap; he kept only the spade, and leaned on it. “Oh,” he thinks, “I was too greedy; I’ve ruined everything; I won’t get there before sunset.” And his fear made him even more breathless. Pakhom runs; his shirt and trousers cling to his body with sweat; his mouth is parched. His chest heaves like a blacksmith’s bellows, his heart beats like a hammer, and his legs are no longer his own: they are giving way. Pakhom was terrified. He thinks: “What if I die of the strain?”

He is afraid of dying, but he cannot stop. “After running all this way,” he thinks, “if I stop now, they’ll call me a fool.” He ran and ran, and was getting close, when he hears the Bashkirs shrieking and shouting to him, and their shouting makes his heart burn even more. Pakhom runs with the last of his strength, and the sun is already near the edge; it has gone into the haze and has grown large and red, the colour of blood. Any moment now it will begin to set. The sun is close to setting, but the starting place is no longer far. Now Pakhom can see the people on the hill waving their arms at him, urging him on. He sees the fox-fur cap on the ground and sees the money on it; and he sees the chief sitting on the ground, holding his belly with his hands. And Pakhom remembered his dream. “There’s plenty of land,” he thinks, “but will God let me live on it? Oh, I’ve ruined myself,” he thinks. “I won’t get there.”

Pakhom looked at the sun, and it had reached the earth; it had begun to set at the edge, and only an arc of it was left above the line. Pakhom summoned the last of his strength and threw his body forward; his legs could barely keep up to stop him falling. Pakhom ran up to the foot of the hill, and suddenly it grew dark. He looked round: the sun had already set. Pakhom gasped. “All my labour is lost,” he thinks. He was about to stop, but he hears the Bashkirs still shouting, and he remembered that from down here it only looks to him as if the sun has set, but from the top of the hill it has not set yet. Pakhom took a deep breath and ran up the hill. On the hill it was still light. Pakhom ran up and sees the cap. In front of the cap sits the chief, cackling with laughter and holding his belly with his hands. Pakhom remembered his dream, cried out, his legs gave way, and he fell forward, and reached the cap with his hands.
“Ah, well done!” cried the chief. “You have won a great deal of land!”
Pakhom’s labourer ran up and tried to lift him, but blood was flowing from his mouth, and he lay dead.
The Bashkirs clicked their tongues in pity.
The labourer picked up the spade, dug a grave for Pakhom exactly as long as he measured from his feet to his head, six feet, and buried him.
